angle: The best outbound plays aren't the templated ones. They're the weird, nuanced ones.
post_first_line: The best outbound signals are the weird ones.
linkedin_post:
The best outbound signals are the weird ones.

Skyler Mickunas sees a pattern in which customer use cases actually work best, and it's not the templated ones.

Delve, a partner seeing a lot of success, wanted to know whether a target account is already SOC 2 compliant. That's not an out-of-the-box signal most teams would find valuable.

But for Delve, it's exactly the right one.

That's also why there isn't a full library of templated use cases. It would be a lot of work, and not all of them would apply to the average user.

Some of the most successful use cases are the most nuanced. Custom signals are a bit of a black box once you open them up.

The signal that wins for you may look useless to everyone else.

What's the weirdest signal your team has ever used?

lesson.title: Why nuanced signals beat templated plays
takeaways: Some of the most successful customer use cases are the most nuanced ones.
A signal can be hugely valuable to one company and irrelevant to most others.
Templated use cases won't cover everything, and not all would apply to the average user.
lesson.exercise: Write down one question about your target accounts that only your business cares about (like whether they already have a specific compliance in place), then work out how you could detect the answer and use it as a signal.

caption: Weird signals win outbound

angle: We track about 100 signals, but the rep decides what to do with each one
post_first_line: Close to 100 signals. Zero one-size-fits-all plays.
linkedin_post:
Close to 100 signals. Zero one-size-fits-all plays.

The signals aren't the interesting part. What happens after one fires is.

We track probably close to 100 signals. When a company hits one, it gets routed to a rep, and the rep chooses the path.

Sometimes that's an auto email, with phone call and LinkedIn tasks layered in so the rep can work from Unify.

Sometimes it's a manual email where we hand the rep all the context, and they tailor something specific. A sniper shot.

Sometimes it's a different alert entirely.

We don't force one workflow on everyone. We start with the workflow the rep wants and work backwards from there.

The goal is to maximize our share on each prospect and account.

Signals tell you when to act. The rep still decides how.

How much control do your reps have over signal plays?
carousel: Slide 1: We track close to 100 signals. Reps still choose the play.
Slide 2: A signal fires and gets routed straight to a rep.
Slide 3: Path one: auto email, plus phone and LinkedIn tasks.
Slide 4: Path two: manual email with full context for a sniper shot.
Slide 5: Path three: a different alert, based on what the rep wants.
Slide 6: We work backwards from the rep's desired workflow.
Slide 7: The goal is maximum share on each prospect and account.
Slide 8: Signals say when to act. Reps decide how.

lesson.title: Let reps choose the play for each signal
takeaways: Routing a signal to a rep beats forcing every signal into one automated sequence.
Different signals call for different plays: auto email, manual sniper shot, or an alert.
Work backwards from the workflow the rep wants to maximize share of each account.
lesson.exercise: List your top 5 signals. For each one, write down the play a rep would pick (auto email, manual sniper shot, or alert), then check whether your routing supports that choice.

caption: 100 signals, rep picks the play

angle: Our rule: if a rep owns the account, it never goes into an automated play
post_first_line: Account ownership beats every number below.
linkedin_post:
Account ownership beats every number below.

200 accounts per AE. 500 to 600 per MBR.

Our outbound runs on one rule: if a rep owns an account, it never goes into an automated play.

Here's how our setup works. Each account executive owns around 200 accounts. Each MBR owns around 500 to 600. We also have shared accounts based on segment, and an inbound MBR who handles the warmer, inbound-driven signals.

The automated plays run outside all of that. They go after accounts nobody owns, find signals where it's relevant, and look for companies that might be a good fit for Unify.

But when a signal fires on an owned account, it doesn't get funneled into a sequence. It goes straight to the rep who owns it.

Say Audrey, an MBR on our team, owns an account. We don't automate against it. We route Audrey the signal, and Audrey decides what to do with it based on how Audrey likes to work.

Automation should fill the gaps in coverage, not override the people who own the relationship.

How do you handle owned accounts in your automations?
carousel: Slide 1: Account ownership trumps every automated play we run.
Slide 2: Each AE owns around 200 accounts.
Slide 3: Each MBR owns around 500 to 600 accounts.
Slide 4: An inbound MBR handles the warmer, inbound-driven signals.
Slide 5: Automated plays run outside all owned accounts.
Slide 6: Signal fires on an owned account? It goes to the rep.
Slide 7: The rep decides what to do, based on their setup.
Slide 8: Automation fills coverage gaps. It never overrides ownership.

lesson.title: Let account ownership override automation
takeaways: Automated plays should target accounts no rep owns, not compete with reps for owned ones.
When a signal hits an owned account, route it to the owner instead of enrolling it in a sequence.
Let reps decide how to act on signals, based on their own preferred setup.
lesson.exercise: Audit your current automated plays this week and check whether any of them are touching accounts a rep owns. Add an exclusion rule, then route those signals to the owner as alerts instead.

caption: Ownership beats automation. Always.

angle: Why we tell our AEs not to automate their outreach
post_first_line: Skyler Mickunas tells AEs to skip automated outreach.
linkedin_post:
Skyler Mickunas tells AEs to skip automated outreach.

The reason has to do with where automation actually belongs.

At Unify, AEs are encouraged to run automated plays that pick up signals, like new hires at target accounts. The automation sits upstream, surfacing the moment.

But at the engagement level, the AE takes over. Because AEs have a strong grasp of the value prop and what different decision makers care about, they send a much lower volume of outreach that converts at a much higher rate.

So our AEs are closed lost circle back specialists. A prospect says the timing is off, and the AE sets a reminder. Then the prospect mentions hiring a head of demand gen, and that's the cue to reach back out.

If AEs started running automated email sequences instead, it would be a worse use of their time. Skyler's team calls the better alternative sniper work.

Automated sequences are something Ethan can replicate, so AEs should spend their time on the work only a human with context can do.

Where do you draw the line on automation?
carousel: Slide 1: We tell our AEs to avoid automating engagement.
Slide 2: Automating signals is encouraged, like new hires at target accounts.
Slide 3: Automation finds the moment. The AE owns the conversation.
Slide 4: AEs know what each decision maker cares about.
Slide 5: That means lower volume, much higher converting outreach.
Slide 6: Our AEs are closed lost circle back specialists.
Slide 7: Timing's off? Set a reminder and return when they hire.
Slide 8: Automated sequences are replicable. Sniper work is the better use of time.

lesson.title: Automate the signal, not the conversation
takeaways: Use automation to detect signals like new hires at target accounts.
AEs with deep value prop knowledge win with low-volume, high-converting outreach.
Closed lost deals are best revived with well-timed, personal follow-up.
lesson.exercise: List your current outreach plays and mark each as signal detection or engagement. Keep automation on the first, and move the second back to a human with a reminder tied to a trigger.

caption: Don't automate your AEs

angle: Pushing reps from 300 to 1,000 accounts a week just makes conversion pay the price
post_first_line: 500 to 1,000 accounts a week per rep.
linkedin_post:
500 to 1,000 accounts a week per rep.

That's the volume some teams expect, and it quietly breaks the thing they care about most.

Skyler Mickunas sees it as naive to expect a human rep to work that many accounts as diligently as they'd work 200 to 300 accounts a week.

Push volume expectations too high on individual reps and conversion on average activity pays the price.

And the goal is the outcome. If volume goes up and conversion goes down, the outcome probably doesn't move in any meaningful way.

So at Unify, we have reps working about 500 to 600 accounts per month, diligently. That gives enough tender loving care to each individual outbound effort.

Skyler is clear that this math will vary case by case. The principle holds: more volume doesn't buy more results if quality drops.

What's your rep's real account capacity?

Slide 2: Expecting 500 to 1,000 accounts a week is naive.
Slide 3: Reps work 200 to 300 accounts a week far more diligently.
Slide 4: Push volume too high and conversion pays the price.
Slide 5: Volume up, conversion down: the outcome barely moves.
Slide 6: Our reps work about 500 to 600 accounts a month.
Slide 7: That leaves real care in every outbound effort.
Slide 8: The math varies by team. Optimize for outcomes, not activity.

lesson.title: Volume Isn't the Outcome
takeaways: Expecting reps to work 500 to 1,000 accounts a week at the same diligence as 200 to 300 is unrealistic.
When volume rises and conversion falls, the outcome barely moves.
Set account load so each outbound effort gets real attention; Unify's reps work about 500 to 600 accounts a month.
lesson.exercise: Pull your reps' account counts and conversion rates side by side. Find the load level where conversion starts to drop, and set your target capacity just below it.

caption: More accounts, worse conversion

angle: What Ethan and I work together on is we've got 10,000 accounts.
linkedin_post:
10,000 accounts. Coverage on 6,000.

The other 4,000 are where the real decision gets made.

Skyler Mickunas works with Ethan on a target list of 10,000 accounts. With the current team, they can reasonably get really good coverage over about 6,000 of them.

Too much AI and automation, and the conversion rate pays the price. Too much manual human effort, and you run into a coverage gap. Everybody wants a fully automatic sniper rifle, but that does not exist.

So Ethan does the growth and RevOps work to figure out that not every account on the list is equally attractive. Then Skyler and Ethan split the list: tier 1 and tier 2 make up the top half, and everything else needs automated coverage.

As human headcount scales, the team can attack more of that tier 1 and tier 2 bucket by hand.

The goal isn't to automate everything or to touch everything personally. It's to decide which accounts earn a human and which ones get a system.

How do you decide which accounts get a human?
carousel: Slide 1: 10,000 target accounts. Coverage on about 6,000.
Slide 2: Too much automation and conversion rate pays the price.
Slide 3: Too much manual effort and you hit a coverage gap.
Slide 4: The fully automatic sniper rifle does not exist.
Slide 5: Not every account on your list is equally attractive.
Slide 6: Tier 1 and tier 2 get the human attention.
Slide 7: Everything else gets automated coverage.
Slide 8: As headcount grows, humans take on more of the top tiers.

lesson.title: Split your account list between humans and automation
takeaways: Too much automation hurts conversion, and too much manual work creates a coverage gap.
Not every account on a target list is equally attractive, so tier the list.
Tier 1 and tier 2 get human effort, the rest gets automated coverage, and humans take on more as headcount scales.
lesson.exercise: Take your target account list and rank it. Mark the top half as tier 1 and tier 2, then write down how each remaining account will get automated coverage.
